prompt: Which statement compares the transport service TCP and UDP give an application?
options: TCP supplies an ordered byte stream; UDP supplies separate datagrams.
TCP preserves each application write; UDP combines writes into a byte stream.
TCP guarantees application success; UDP reports whether the service accepted data.
TCP encrypts its data by default; UDP relies on application encryption.
explanation: TCP delivers an ordered, recovered byte stream, while UDP delivers separate datagrams with no delivery guarantee. Message framing and encryption are the application’s concern.

whyWrong.1: TCP does not preserve write boundaries, and UDP does not make a byte stream.
whyWrong.2: Transport delivery does not mean the application finished its work.
whyWrong.3: Neither TCP nor UDP encrypts data by default.

prompt: Which comparison distinguishes TCP flow control from congestion control?
options: Flow control tracks network loss; congestion control advertises receiver space.
Flow control respects receiver capacity; congestion control responds to the path.
Flow control establishes a connection; congestion control closes each direction.
Flow control selects service ports; congestion control identifies application data.
explanation: Flow control uses the receiver’s advertised window to match receiver capacity. Congestion control slows the sender in response to network-path conditions.

whyWrong.0: This reverses the receiver and network roles.
whyWrong.2: Opening and closing a connection are separate TCP functions.
whyWrong.3: Ports identify endpoints; they do not control receiver capacity or congestion.

prompt: Which two services conventionally use TCP? Choose two.
options: Initial DHCPv4 discovery
SMTP server-to-server mail transfer
NTP time synchronization
SSH remote management
explanation: SMTP uses TCP 25 and SSH uses TCP 22. DHCPv4 discovery and NTP conventionally use UDP.

whyWrong.0: DHCPv4 discovery uses UDP ports 68 and 67.

prompt: Which two statements correctly describe DNS transport? Choose two.
options: DNS queries can use UDP destination port 53.
TCP port 53 is reserved exclusively for zone transfers.
DNS queries can use TCP destination port 53.
A UDP DNS query first establishes a UDP transport connection.
explanation: DNS uses both UDP 53 and TCP 53. Small queries usually use UDP, and TCP carries queries that need it, such as retries after a truncated UDP response.

whyWrong.1: TCP 53 also carries ordinary queries, not just zone transfers.

prompt: Which endpoint interpretation follows from this TCP opening?
options: The server requests a service on TCP 51514 at 10.20.0.15.
The server listens on TCP 9000 and the client selects TCP 3000.
The client requests TCP 22 at 10.20.0.5 from local port 51514.
The client requests TCP 22 and receives replies on local port 22.
explanation: The SYN goes from client port 51514 to server port 22, so the client is requesting SSH. Replies reverse the ports, and the displayed sequence numbers are not ports.

whyWrong.0: The SYN sender is the client and 22 is the destination service.
whyWrong.1: 9000 and 3000 are sequence numbers, not ports.
whyWrong.3: The server replies to the client’s port 51514, not 22.

prompt: A DHCPv4 client has no usable IPv4 address and begins discovery. Which initial transport exchange matches this task?
options: UDP source port 67 to destination port 68, sent by the new client.
TCP source port 68 to destination port 67, after a TCP opening.
UDP source port 68 to destination port 53, requesting its address.
UDP source port 68 to destination port 67, which can be broadcast.
explanation: DHCPv4 discovery is UDP from client port 68 to server port 67. It can be broadcast before the client has an address and needs no TCP opening.

whyWrong.0: This reverses the client and server ports.

prompt: A client opens two simultaneous TCP connections to the same server address on TCP 443. What distinguishes the two connections?
options: The server uses a different listening port for the second connection.
The client uses a different local source port for the second connection.
The client uses a different TCP protocol number for the second connection.
The server uses a different MAC address for the second connection.
explanation: The client uses a different source port for each connection, so each has a distinct address-and-port pair. One server listening port serves many connections.

whyWrong.0: Both connections use the server’s port 443.
whyWrong.2: Both use TCP, so the protocol number is the same.
whyWrong.3: MAC addresses are not part of a transport connection’s identity.

exhibit.title: Representative application writes
exhibit.text:
Write 1: 200 bytes
Write 2: 300 bytes
Transport: TCP

prompt: The application makes the writes shown. What must its receiving application assume?
options: It receives a byte stream and must use its message format to find boundaries.
It receives two messages whose boundaries match the two sending writes.
It receives a message boundary wherever the TCP PSH flag is present.
It receives one application message for each arriving TCP segment.
explanation: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream, not the sender’s write boundaries. The application must use its own framing, such as a length or delimiter.

whyWrong.1: Two writes need not arrive as two separate messages.
whyWrong.2: The PSH flag does not mark application message boundaries.
whyWrong.3: A message can span segments, and a segment can hold several messages.

spec.title: Complete the TCP opening
spec.caption: No application data is included in the opening segments.

prompt: The client has received the second segment. Which third segment completes this ordinary TCP opening?
options: Server to client: FIN, ending the server’s sending direction.
Client to server: SYN, starting another independent connection.
Server to client: ACK, acknowledging its own initial sequence.
Client to server: ACK, acknowledging the server’s SYN.
explanation: After the server’s SYN/ACK, the client sends an ACK for the server’s SYN, completing SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK.

whyWrong.0: FIN closes a direction; it does not complete the opening.
whyWrong.1: A new SYN would start another connection.
whyWrong.2: The client must acknowledge the server’s SYN, not the server.

prompt: A TCP data segment begins at sequence 20001 and contains 1460 bytes, with no SYN or FIN. All earlier bytes arrived in order and no later data is buffered. Which cumulative acknowledgment follows?
explanation: The segment covers sequence numbers 20001–21460, so the cumulative ACK is the next expected byte, 21461.

whyWrong.2: 21460 is the last byte received, not the next expected.
whyWrong.3: Only SYN or FIN consume an extra sequence number, and neither is present.

exhibit.title: Representative Windows netstat -an excerpt
exhibit.text:
Proto  Local Address         Foreign Address        State
TCP    0.0.0.0:22            0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING
TCP    172.16.5.20:22        172.16.5.99:50210       ESTABLISHED
TCP    172.16.5.20:50344     198.51.100.10:443       ESTABLISHED
TCP    172.16.5.20:50351     198.51.100.10:443       TIME_WAIT

prompt: SSH uses local TCP 22 and HTTPS uses remote TCP 443. Which reading of this snapshot is correct?
options: Two HTTPS connections are established, and the local host initiates SSH.
The local host has one SSH listener but no accepted SSH connection.
The local host serves HTTPS and connects outward from SSH port 22.
One SSH connection is accepted and one HTTPS connection is established.
explanation: The local port-22 row is an accepted SSH connection, and only the port-50344 HTTPS row is ESTABLISHED. The other HTTPS row is in TIME_WAIT.

whyWrong.0: TIME_WAIT is not ESTABLISHED, and local port 22 is the server side.
whyWrong.1: The ESTABLISHED port-22 row is an accepted connection.
whyWrong.2: Local port 22 is the server endpoint, and the local HTTPS port is the client’s temporary port.

prompt: What does this client-side observation establish about the connection attempt?
options: The attempt received an active reset and did not complete a TCP opening.
The opening completed, but an established session then timed out.
The SYN was acknowledged normally and the client should send login data.
The request received no response before its retransmission timer expired.
explanation: The RST/ACK reply is an active rejection, so no TCP opening completed. The capture does not show whether the server or something on the path sent the reset.

whyWrong.1: No SYN/ACK and final ACK appear, so no connection was established.
whyWrong.2: A reset is not a SYN/ACK acceptance.
whyWrong.3: A reply was received, so this is not silence.

prompt: The receiver has all earlier bytes and retains the shown later range. Which cumulative acknowledgment stays in place, and when may it advance to 1301?
options: 1301 now; the arrival of the highest-numbered range proves all earlier bytes.
1201 now; only another copy of 1201–1300 allows the acknowledgment to advance.
1101 now; receiving the missing 1101–1200 range completes the contiguous data.
1001 now; every original segment must be received again in its original order.
explanation: A cumulative ACK cannot skip a gap, so it stays at 1101 until the missing 1101–1200 arrives. Then the buffered later bytes complete the stream through 1300 and the ACK advances to 1301.

whyWrong.0: Later bytes do not prove the earlier gap arrived.
whyWrong.3: The earlier and later ranges are already held and need not be resent.

exhibit.title: Representative combined client evidence
exhibit.text:
Approved server: 192.168.40.20, HTTP on TCP 80
Fresh DNS answer www.lab.test: 192.168.40.20
Ping 192.168.40.20: replies received
TCP capture at client: SYN to 192.168.40.20:80; retry SYN; no reply seen
Fresh HTTP request: fails

prompt: All tests are fresh and target the intended server. Which next investigation best fits the combined evidence?
options: Correct DNS first because the browser used a name rather than an address.
Correct the client subnet because TCP and ICMP require different gateways.
Check TCP 80 service and path evidence; ICMP success does not prove the opening.
Begin HTTP content diagnosis because a successful ping proves TCP acceptance.
explanation: The name lookup and ping succeed, but the capture shows no completed TCP opening. Check the TCP 80 listener and the path.

whyWrong.0: The name response already returns the approved server address.
whyWrong.1: Different transports do not imply a different gateway or subnet.
whyWrong.3: A ping does not perform the TCP opening.

prompt: What is the minimum size of a TCP header?
options: 8 bytes
20 bytes
32 bytes
64 bytes
explanation: The TCP header is at least 20 bytes. UDP’s header is 8 bytes.

whyWrong.2: 32 bytes is not the TCP minimum.
whyWrong.3: 64 bytes is not a TCP header size in this chapter.

prompt: How wide is a TCP or UDP port field, and what values can it hold?
explanation: Each port field is 16 bits, so values run from 0 to 65535. Port 0 is reserved.

whyWrong.2: A 16-bit field holds up to 65535, not 1024.
whyWrong.3: 32 bits is the width of an IPv4 address and of TCP sequence numbers, not ports.

prompt: What is the relationship between TCP port 53 and UDP port 53?
options: They are separate transport endpoints
They are the same endpoint
UDP 53 is a backup for TCP 53
Only one can be open at a time
explanation: TCP and UDP have separate port spaces, so TCP 53 and UDP 53 are different endpoints.

whyWrong.1: The two protocols do not share a port space.
whyWrong.2: Neither port is a backup; each is its own endpoint.
whyWrong.3: Both can be open on the same host at once.

prompt: Which statement about ICMP echo (ping) is correct?
options: It uses no ports and has no TCP handshake
It uses TCP port 7 for each request
It uses UDP port 1 for each request
It completes a SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK exchange
explanation: ICMP echo does not use TCP or UDP ports and performs no TCP handshake, so a successful ping does not prove a TCP service works.

whyWrong.1: ICMP is not carried over TCP and has no ports.
whyWrong.2: ICMP is not carried over UDP and has no ports.
whyWrong.3: The SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK handshake belongs to TCP.
